analysis.one_liner: Bans federal agencies from using facial recognition and biometric surveillance unless Congress explicitly authorizes it, and cuts law enforcement grants to states and cities that use it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it unlawful for any federal agency, or any government contractor, to acquire or use facial recognition or other biometric identification — like face, voice, or gait scanning — unless Congress first passed a law specifically authorizing that exact use, with strict accuracy and due-process requirements. Evidence obtained in violation would be unusable in federal proceedings, and individuals could sue. It would also have cut federal Byrne law-enforcement grants to states and cities that don't adopt similar bans. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone whose face, voice, or movements could be scanned by the government — essentially all Americans. The bill would have required Congress to openly authorize and regulate any specific government use of facial recognition before it happens, banned federal purchase of the technology in the meantime, made illegally gathered biometric evidence inadmissible, and given individuals the right to sue for damages. People most affected are those disproportionately misidentified by the technology, including people with darker skin and women, since the bill required accuracy audits broken down by gender and skin color before any authorized use.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for any federal agency or official to acquire or use facial recognition or other remote biometric identification unless Congress passes a law explicitly authorizing that specific use, with accuracy audits and due-process protections written in.
Evidence obtained in violation of the ban cannot be used against people in federal proceedings, and individuals can sue the federal government for damages when their faces are scanned illegally.

States and cities that want to keep using the technology lose federal Byrne law-enforcement grants unless they adopt matching bans, spreading the protection down to the local level where most police face-scanning happens.

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies, which would lose access to facial recognition for identifying suspects and would face grant cuts unless they adopted matching bans. Biometric surveillance vendors would lose government customers and be barred from selling federal services.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not just regulate misuse of facial recognition — it bans federal agencies from using it at all unless Congress later passes a law specifically authorizing each use, which would deprive police of a tool used to find missing children, identify crime suspects, and verify identities at airports.

The condition on Byrne grant money pressures state and local governments to pass matching bans or lose federal public-safety funding, which overrides local choices about how to police their own communities.

The private sector is untouched: the moratorium covers government use, so companies could still build and sell face-scanning products and amass biometric data, arguably the largest source of the privacy concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost is to law enforcement effectiveness: police would lose a tool for identifying suspects, missing persons, and scanning surveillance footage, and critics argue facial recognition can be used responsibly with strict rules rather than a near-total ban. The bill answers this by allowing Congress to authorize specific uses later, with accuracy audits and due-process protections, but its default is a moratorium rather than a regulatory framework. The privacy and civil-liberties benefit — preventing mass, largely unregulated tracking of faces and voices — is substantial; the enforcement cost is real but avoidable through the bill's authorization pathway.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 7, 2023, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government agencies and biometric vendors that wanted to keep using facial recognition, since the ban never arrived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies and biometric tech vendors

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Sens. Merkley, Warren, Sanders, and Wyden

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote.

against.name: Law enforcement and biometric technology industry
against.role: Federal, state, and local police agencies and facial recognition vendors
against.what_they_did: Have an institutional interest in continuing to use and sell facial recognition tools; such interests commonly oppose moratorium bills, though no opposition by them to this bill appears in the provided record.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Democrats or the independent Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-led Senate Judiciary Committee.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance vendors
industries.note: Federal agencies would be barred from buying or using their products, and federal funds could not pay for them, cutting off a major government customer base until Congress authorizes specific uses. State and local pressure via grant conditions would shrink the market further.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local)
industries.note: Federal agencies lose a tool used for identifying suspects and screening travelers; state and local police face a choice between the same ban and losing Byrne grant money. Some agencies would gain certainty about what is allowed.
